title: Redwood discovery — reliability & fallbacks with Bluehaven Retail

Fallback policies and model variant routing

header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Lucas Moreno (Redwood SE), Mark Torres (CTO, Bluehaven), Aisha Khan (Head of Infra), Ben Liu (Product), Sofia Ortega (SRE)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Jordan from Redwood. We're here to understand your reliability and incident tolerance requirements for the LLM parts of the platform.
[00:08] Mark Torres: Thanks Jordan. Quick context — we run low-latency product search and a recommendations microservice that uses embeddings and generative re-ranking. We care a lot about availability during peak shopping windows.
[00:20] Aisha Khan: Yeah, outages during Black Friday are a non-starter. We need clear fallback rules when model endpoints are degraded.
[00:27] Priya Shah: Totally. Before we dive in, can you share current traffic patterns? p95/p99 latency targets?
[00:33] Ben Liu: Typical QPS for the search endpoint is 130 qps steady with 800 qps peaks. Target p95 latency is under 200ms; p99 ideally under 450ms for user-facing requests. For batch offline stuff, we don't care as much.
[00:48] Sofia Ortega: Also, our infra is multi-region — us-east-1 primary, us-west-2 as standby. We want routing that prefers region-local inference but can fail over gracefully.
[00:58] Jordan Kim: Great — that helps. At a high level, Redwood supports Hosted (our managed API), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools for you), and Private (VPC/on-prem). Each has different controls for routing, caching, and fallbacks.
[01:12] Lucas Moreno: For incident tolerance, the common patterns are: 1) model variant fallback (e.g., big -> quantized or smaller model), 2) cached prefix or KV responses for hot prompts, 3) multi-region routing with health checks and automatic failover, and 4) graceful degradation to non-LLM or simpler heuristics.
[01:34] Mark Torres: Can you explain how model variant fallback works in practice? We don't want sudden quality drops to impact conversions.
[01:41] Priya Shah: Sure — you define a routing policy attached to each logical route. When latency or error rates exceed thresholds, the router can fallback to a compatible model family with a lower compute profile. We give you SLO-based thresholds and can do gradual roll-forward: first we can reduce concurrency, then switch to a quantized variant, then to a smaller architecture.
[02:02] Aisha Khan: Is that automatic or manual?
[02:04] Priya Shah: It can be both. For Hosted customers many use automated policies with alerting. For Dedicated/Private, you can set stricter controls — automatic fallbacks with approval gates, or manual escalation with runbook hooks.
[02:16] Mark Torres: And across regions — if us-east saturates, how quickly does traffic switch to us-west?
[02:21] Lucas Moreno: We do active health checking and keep region-aware pools. Failover latency depends on the detection window and cold-start costs. Typical detection and routing switch can be under 10s for network blips; for capacity pressure that requires spin-up, you might see longer, so we use pre-warmed pools for critical routes.
[02:36] Sofia Ortega: Pre-warmed pools — what's the footprint? We can't reserve massive GPUs for standby.
[02:41] Jordan Kim: With Dedicated you choose reserved capacity and burst policies. For mission-critical routes we recommend a small warm standby in secondary region sized for typical burst; combined with a smaller-model fallback to handle overflow. That keeps cost predictable without dedicating a full fleet.
[02:56] Aisha Khan: We also need auditability and ability to prove we failed over during an incident for postmortems.
[03:01] Priya Shah: Redwood Console records per-route events, routing decisions, and fallback triggers. We emit traces and logs you can ingest into your SIEM. We also keep token-level cost and latency breakdowns to explain the why.
[03:13] Ben Liu: Can you tie SLOs to billing? For example, if you miss our uptime SLA, what's the credit structure?
[03:20] Jordan Kim: For Hosted we publish uptime SLAs in the contract. Dedicated contracts can include stricter SLAs with service credits. Exact terms depend on commitment level; we'll share sample SLO docs.
[03:30] Mark Torres: Regarding data residency, some of our PII must stay in-region. Does Redwood support region-restricted routing so inference never leaves the EU or a given region?
[03:38] Priya Shah: Yes — routing policies can be constrained by region and by model placement. For Private deployments you control the entire network so you can ensure inference never leaves your VPC. For Hosted we support region pinning and have controls for data residency, but you'll want Dedicated or Private if strict in-region processing is mandated.
[03:54] Sofia Ortega: How do you handle KV/prefix caching for recommendations? If we cache top-k lists, we can avoid hitting the model for common queries.
[04:01] Lucas Moreno: Redwood provides automatic prefix/KV caching; you can set TTLs and cacheable keys. For recommendation endpoints we often cache reranks for popular items for short windows (tens of seconds) to massively reduce token counts and latency. We can also do stale-while-revalidate to avoid blocking user requests while refreshing cached outputs.
[04:18] Aisha Khan: What about consistency — if a product goes out of stock, we can't serve stale recs.
[04:22] Priya Shah: You can attach cache invalidation hooks to your inventory events, or set short TTLs and use real-time signals to bypass cache. Redwood's caching layer integrates with webhook invalidation and pub/sub patterns.
[04:32] Mark Torres: In an incident scenario, do you recommend falling back to a deterministic non-ML path?
[04:36] Jordan Kim: Yes — for critical call paths, a hybrid approach is best: primary LLM path with fallbacks to cached responses, smaller models, and finally deterministic heuristics. We see customers map each endpoint to a criticality score and codify policies per score.
[04:49] Ben Liu: Can we get examples of thresholds you use?
[04:51] Priya Shah: Typical policy: if p95 latency > 500ms for 2 minutes or error rate > 3% for 1 minute, trigger rollout to quantized variant; if p95 > 800ms or error rate > 5% for 1 minute, route to smaller model or cache; if region health < 60% then route traffic to other region with pre-warm if available. We can tune numbers to your risk profile.
[05:12] Sofia Ortega: How do you measure health — by infrastructure metrics or application error semantics?
[05:16] Lucas Moreno: Multiple signals: infra (GPU utilization, queue lengths), app (model timeouts, error codes), and user-facing metrics (response latencies). Routing decisions can be made with weighted combinations so you don't overreact to noisy metrics.
[05:27] Mark Torres: For Dedicated, do we get isolated GPU pools? We want predictable p99.
[05:32] Jordan Kim: Yes — Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, configurable autoscaling, and burst policies. You can set per-pool concurrency limits and Redwood will enforce request shaping to preserve p99 targets.
[05:42] Aisha Khan: If we run Dedicated in our VPC (Private), who manages patching and kernel updates?
[05:47] Priya Shah: For Private on-prem, you manage the host OS and networking; Redwood's control plane can be run as a customer-managed instance or a hybrid where we handle orchestration. We can propose a managed service add-on if you want Redwood to handle infra ops.
[05:58] Ben Liu: On the subject of model cold-starts — if a model isn't in cache in the standby region, what's the expected hit?
[06:04] Lucas Moreno: Cold-start depends on model size and quantization; for a 13B model it can be tens of seconds if you need to load weights. That's why pre-warmed pools or smaller-variant fallback reduces user impact. For many customers, pre-warm minimal workers plus async fallback is the sweet spot.
[06:18] Mark Torres: How does the router decide split during partial degradation? Suppose us-east is 80% healthy — do you send a fixed percentage to us-west?
[06:26] Priya Shah: We support weighted routing and can do gradual traffic draining. In partial degradation we typically shift a percentage of traffic determined by policy and observed error budgets; you can define a linear ramp to avoid thundering herd.
[06:37] Aisha Khan: Do we get raw traces and decision logs for every fallback decision? We need that for audits.
[06:42] Jordan Kim: Yes, Redwood Console exposes decision logs, and you can stream those to your SIEM or S3. Each entry includes timestamp, trigger metric, previous model, chosen fallback, and routing weights.
[06:54] Ben Liu: What about test harnesses — can we simulate region outages during a PoC?
[06:58] Lucas Moreno: Absolutely — we'll run chaos drills during the benchmark. We can simulate region failover, saturated GPU pools, and inject timeouts to validate your runbooks.
[07:08] Mark Torres: SLA specifics — for Dedicated, what's the uptime % and credits?
[07:12] Jordan Kim: Sample Dedicated SLA is 99.9% monthly for provisioned capacity; credits scale by downtime minutes and severity. We tailor legal terms in the enterprise contract and can share a sample SLA attachment.
[07:24] Aisha Khan: Are there any single points of control plane failure if we do Private?
[07:29] Priya Shah: In Private you control the control plane deployment pattern. We recommend active-active control plane across two AZs or regions. Redwood can provide an HA deployment topology for the control plane and operator scripts.
[07:40] Ben Liu: Security question: how are keys managed if we do Dedicated in our cloud?
[07:44] Jordan Kim: We integrate with customer KMS/HSM for model keys and encryption-at-rest. For Dedicated in customer's cloud, keys remain under your KMS. For Hosted we offer dedicated keyspaces and BYOK options.
[07:55] Sofia Ortega: Any limitations on model uploads or custom containers in Private?
[07:59] Priya Shah: Private supports custom model artifacts and container images subject to sizing and compatibility. We have an onboarding checklist. For very large models we run a compatibility pass and recommend quantization profiles.
[08:10] Mark Torres: Cost — how do fallbacks affect billing? If we route to a larger host for some requests, does cost jump?
[08:16] Lucas Moreno: Billing is per-token compute and instance-hours for Dedicated. Fallbacks to larger models will increase token compute costs for those requests. Our Optimize tooling can simulate cost impact and suggest where caching or smaller-model fallbacks reduce unit costs.
[08:29] Ben Liu: Could Redwood automatically switch back to the primary when the region recovers?
[08:33] Priya Shah: Yes — policy can be auto-recover with hysteresis so we wait for sustained healthy metrics before moving traffic back. That prevents flapping.
[08:42] Mark Torres: For our internal incident runbooks, we'll need exact event IDs and timestamps. Confirm those are provided.
[08:47] Jordan Kim: Confirmed — every routing decision and fallback is logged with IDs you can reference in postmortem.
[08:54] Aisha Khan: One more — do you have recommendations for throttling client-side when the model is degraded?
[08:59] Lucas Moreno: Yes, we suggest adaptive client-side retry with exponential backoff, and a circuit-breaker that uses a degradation signal from the router. For user-facing low-latency calls, prefer soft-fail to simpler heuristics rather than retries that add latency.
[09:12] Ben Liu: Next steps: we'd like a benchmark with our traffic shape and a PoC to test failover.
[09:17] Jordan Kim: We'll share a short benchmark plan. Priya — can you own the test script and coordinate with Aisha on traffic replay?
[09:22] Priya Shah: Yep — I'll put together load profiles and the failover scenarios.
[09:25] Mark Torres: Also send the security whitepaper and sample SLA so legal can review.
[09:29] Jordan Kim: Will do. Any other questions?
[09:31] Sofia Ortega: Not for now. We'll sync after you send the materials.
[09:33] Jordan Kim: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pricing, SLA, security docs, and schedule the technical deep-dive.
[09:39] End of recording: approximate.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts — product names sometimes mis-transcribed (e.g., 'KV cache' became 'kay-vee cache' in original auto transcript). References to Redwood Console/Routing policies/Optimize were high-level; deep technical details scheduled for follow-up technical session.
